screens.title: Network Access Control with Cisco ISE
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Control is the practice of verifying and enforcing who and what can connect to your network. In modern enterprise environments, attackers can bypass perimeter controls by plugging into an access port or joining an open Wi-Fi. NAC adds a policy gate at every connection point so only authorized users and compliant devices can gain access. In this lesson you will see the 802.1X authentication model — supplicant, authenticator, and authentication server — and how Cisco Identity Services Engine centralizes policy decisions, posture checks, guest onboarding, and integration with Active Directory. You will also learn practical steps to configure a Cisco switch for 802.1X and MAC Authentication Bypass so legacy devices can still be controlled. We will highlight common mistakes such as wrong RADIUS secrets, blocked ports, or incorrect authentication order that can prevent devices from reaching the network. By the end of this chapter you will understand the components, the workflow, and a clear lab checklist to deploy basic NAC with ISE. Consider: which device types in your network must be treated as 802.1X-capable, and which will need MAB?

Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Overview
Network Access Control with Cisco ISE
Enforce identity and device posture at every network access point using 802.1X and Cisco ISE for centralized policy and reporting.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
NAC: Verify & Enforce

In this lesson

Why this matters
NAC reduces attack surface, enforces compliance, and enables dynamic segmentation based on identity and device posture, which limits lateral movement during incidents.

Use ISE and 802.1X to keep unmanaged IoT devices on a restricted VLAN while giving managed endpoints full network access after posture checks.

Supplicant, Authenticator, Authentication Server

Switch: AAA, RADIUS, dot1x, MAB
Explore Key Topics

ISE Architecture
PAN for policy, PSN for runtime, MnT for logs — combine for scalable authentication and reporting.
MAB & Legacy Devices
When devices lack 802.1X, MAB uses the MAC address as an identity for RADIUS checks and policy decisions.

screens.title: What is Network Access Control and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Control is a security approach that enforces policy each time a device or user attempts to connect to the network. At its core NAC asks two questions: who are you, and is your device compliant? If the answers meet policy, access is granted; if not, access is limited or denied. This prevents unmanaged or compromised devices from freely interacting with critical resources. For instance, if a laptop without updated antivirus plugs into an access switch, NAC can place it in a remediation VLAN until it meets compliance. A common misconception is treating NAC as only an identity check; in practice it combines identity, device posture, location, and time to make context-aware decisions. Another mistake is relying solely on perimeter controls — NAC enforces policy at the edge and reduces lateral movement during incidents. Example: a finance workstation should be placed in a VLAN with stricter access if it fails a posture check. Key takeaway: NAC is a gatekeeper at every access point that enforces who, what, and how devices connect. Consider which device groups in your network should be subject to the strictest NAC rules and why.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › What is NAC?
Definition & purpose
Network Access Control enforces policy at the moment of connection, combining identity and device posture to grant or restrict access. It reduces exposure by ensuring only authorized and compliant endpoints can access sensitive resources.
Analogy
Think of NAC as a security checkpoint that checks ID and health of every device before letting it into the building.
Common misconception
NAC is more than username verification. It enforces device posture, group membership, and contextual attributes like location.
Key Takeaway

NAC limits lateral movement by verifying identity and device health at every access point — making breaches harder to propagate.

Concrete example
A user brings a laptop to the office. The switch places the port in an unauthorized state. The laptop's supplicant sends EAP requests. The switch forwards these in RADIUS to ISE. If the laptop fails a posture check, ISE assigns a remediation VLAN instead of full access.
Why it matters
Prevents unmanaged devices from accessing critical assets and enforces compliance automatically.
Quick policy example
if user in Finance_Group and device.isCompliant:
  assign VLAN 10
  apply finance QoS
else:
  place in remediation VLAN
Check your understanding
Which endpoints on your network would you place in remediation VLANs and why? Consider business risk and device manageability.

screens.title: 802.1X Authentication Flow
screens.narratorSegment: The 802.1X process is a handshake that gates a port until an authentication server trusts the device. First, the supplicant — the client device — initiates EAP messages when it detects a network connection. The authenticator, typically a switch or access point, intercepts those EAP frames and encapsulates them in RADIUS packets to forward to the authentication server. The server, often a RADIUS instance such as Cisco ISE, validates credentials and posture, then returns an Accept, Reject, or some attributes that the authenticator enforces. A key detail is port states: the authenticator keeps the port in an unauthorized state until it receives an Accept. A common example is a laptop that presents machine certificates via EAP-TLS; the server validates the certificate chain before accepting. Misconceptions often arise around who stores credentials — the RADIUS server holds or proxies identity stores, not the switch. Another pitfall is assuming EAP payloads transit unmodified; the authenticator encapsulates them in RADIUS so the server can perform policy mapping. Takeaway: understanding this three-party exchange helps you diagnose failures such as RADIUS rejects, timeouts, or ports stuck unauthorized. Try tracing a failed login: is the supplicant sending EAP, does the switch forward RADIUS, and what does the server log show?

keyIdea.text: 802.1X uses EAP between supplicant and server with the switch relaying RADIUS; the port remains unauthorized until the server accepts.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › 802.1X Flow
Step-by-step flow
1. Supplicant detects network, sends EAP-Start and EAP-Response identity.
2. Authenticator (switch/AP) places port in unauthorized state and forwards EAP in RADIUS to authentication server.
3. Authentication Server validates credentials or posture and returns Access-Accept or Reject with attributes.
4. Authenticator applies attributes and transitions port to authorized if accepted.
Example
A laptop using EAP-TLS sends a certificate; the server verifies chain and returns an Accept that maps the device to a user VLAN.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Confirm supplicant logs show EAP requests being sent.
  • Check switch logs for RADIUS forwarding and shared secret match.
  • Review ISE logs for Accept/Reject and posture results.
  • Watch for ports stuck in unauthorized state and check timeouts.
Common mistake
Assuming the switch performs authentication limits troubleshooting. The switch relays EAP; the server makes the decision.

screens.title: Cisco ISE Components and Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Cisco Identity Services Engine is the centralized platform that makes policy decisions for network access. It separates concerns so each node type handles specific responsibilities. The Policy Administration Node, or PAN, is the management and configuration point where administrators author policies, define user and device profiles, and push configurations. The Policy Service Node — PSN — is the runtime engine that receives RADIUS requests from network devices, performs authentication and authorization, and returns decisions rapidly. For logging and reporting, the Monitoring and Troubleshooting Node, or MnT, collects logs and provides dashboards that help operators debug access issues and audit events. Optionally, Endpoint Protection Services handle additional endpoint security tasks. A common architecture is to place PANs centrally for management and deploy multiple PSNs near branch access points to reduce latency and improve redundancy. A misconception is to expect a single ISE node to handle both management and heavy runtime loads. In production, separating PAN from PSNs and MnT improves scalability and availability. Example: a PSN in a regional datacenter services hundreds of switches and forwards logs to the MnT. Takeaway: map policy administration, enforcement, and monitoring to distinct ISE roles for a scalable NAC deployment.

keyIdea.text: Separate PAN for policy, PSN for runtime enforcement, and MnT for logging to scale NAC across the enterprise.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › ISE Architecture
Components at a glance
Policy Administration Node (PAN)
Central configuration and policy authoring point for ISE.
Policy Service Node (PSN)
Handles authentication, authorization, and accounting in real time.
Monitoring & Troubleshooting (MnT)
Collects logs and provides dashboards for auditing and incident response.
Endpoint Protection Services (EPS)
Optional node for enhanced endpoint posture and protection functions.
Deployment note & example
Separate PAN from PSNs; place PSNs closer to branch switches to reduce RADIUS latency. MnT can be centralized for consolidated logs and reporting.
Example topology
PAN in HQ for policy management, multiple PSNs per region for enforcement, MnT receiving logs centrally for audit and troubleshooting.
Key Takeaway

Separating management, enforcement, and monitoring nodes improves scale, redundancy, and maintainability for enterprise NAC.

screens.title: Switch Configuration Essentials for 802.1X and MAB
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a Cisco switch for 802.1X and MAB begins with the global AAA and RADIUS server setup so the switch can reach ISE. You enable 'aaa new-model', point dot1x authentication to a RADIUS server group, and configure accounting if you need logs for sessions. Next, define the RADIUS server with its IP and shared key so the switch and ISE can communicate. Enabling 'dot1x system-auth-control' turns on 802.1X globally. For interface-specific behavior, set 'authentication port-control auto' to enable port-based control, choose 'authentication host-mode' appropriate to whether you expect phones and PCs on the same port, and set 'authentication order' to prefer dot1x or mab depending on the device mix. The 'mab' command enables MAC Authentication Bypass for legacy devices, and 'dot1x pae authenticator' sets the switch as the authenticator. A concrete example is setting 'authentication order dot1x mab' for a user laptop port, which tries 802.1X first and falls back to MAB if needed. A frequent mistake is mismatched RADIUS shared secrets or firewall rules blocking UDP 1812 and 1813. When you deploy, test with one port and watch ISE and switch logs for clear Accept or Reject messages. What command would you check first if the switch reports no response from the RADIUS server?

keyIdea.title: Configuration focus
keyIdea.text: Global AAA, RADIUS server entries, and per-interface dot1x and mab settings are the building blocks of switch-side NAC.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Switch Config Essentials
Minimal configuration template
aaa new-model
aaa authentication dot1x default group ISE_RADIUS_GROUP
aaa authorization network default group ISE_RADIUS_GROUP
aaa accounting dot1x default start-stop group ISE_RADIUS_GROUP

radius server ISE_SERVER
 address ipv4 10.0.0.20 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
 key CiscoISEKey!

aaa group server radius ISE_RADIUS_GROUP
 server name ISE_SERVER

dot1x system-auth-control

interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description User Laptop Port
 switchport mode access
 authentication port-control auto
 authentication host-mode multi-host
 authentication order dot1x mab
 mab
 dot1x pae authenticator
 spanning-tree portfast
Why these commands
They enable AAA, register the RADIUS server, and configure the interface to attempt 802.1X and MAB appropriately.
Common failure
Mismatched shared keys or blocked UDP ports are frequent causes of authentication failures; verify connectivity and secrets first.
Example scenarios
Laptop port
Use 'authentication order dot1x mab' to prefer 802.1X but allow MAB fallback for devices without supplicants.
Phone/Printer port
Set 'authentication order mab dot1x' or use 'multi-domain' host-mode for voice/data separation where phones use MAB and phones with 802.1X are supported.
Key Takeaway

Start with a single test port, monitor ISE and switch logs, and validate shared secrets and UDP reachability before wide rollout.

screens.title: 802.1X vs MAB — When to use each
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between 802.1X and MAC Authentication Bypass is about device capability and security needs. 802.1X provides strong, credential-based authentication using EAP methods and supports machine certificates and user credentials. It also allows posture assessment and clearer mapping to users and groups. MAB, by contrast, authenticates by MAC address and is intended for devices that cannot run an 802.1X supplicant, such as legacy printers or some IP phones. MAB is simpler but less secure because MAC addresses can be spoofed unless paired with additional checks in ISE. A sensible deployment pattern prioritizes 802.1X for managed endpoints and uses MAB only where necessary. Misconfiguration often comes from ordering authentication attempts incorrectly, which can lock out devices; for example, putting MAB first where you expect 802.1X devices may cause unintended MAB assignments. Example: use 'authentication order dot1x mab' on user laptop ports and 'authentication order mab dot1x' on printer ports. Takeaway: prefer 802.1X for security, reserve MAB for legacy devices, and explicitly document which ports use which order to prevent surprises during troubleshooting. Which device groups in your environment should be upgraded to 802.1X first?

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › 802.1X vs MAB
Comparison table
802.1X
  • Credential-based EAP authentication
  • Supports certificates and posture checks
  • Stronger identity mapping and policy
MAB
  • Authenticates by device MAC address
  • Useful for legacy printers and phones
  • Higher risk of MAC spoofing
Deployment guidance
Use 802.1X for managed endpoints; reserve MAB for devices that cannot run a supplicant, and document authentication order per port.
Concrete scenarios & tips
Laptop ports
Use dot1x first, mab fallback. This preserves strong authentication while allowing devices that fail 802.1X to be identified.
Printer / legacy devices
Prefer 'authentication order mab dot1x' and multi-domain host-mode for voice/data separation where needed.
Mistake to avoid
Allowing MAB by default on many ports increases risk — choose MAB deliberately and audit MAC lists regularly.

screens.title: ISE Integration with Active Directory
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating Cisco ISE with Active Directory lets ISE query user and group attributes to make policy decisions. When ISE receives a RADIUS authentication request, it can perform an LDAP or AD lookup to determine group membership, user account status, and other attributes. This allows policies that say, for example, if a user is a member of 'Finance_Group' and the device posture is compliant, then assign VLAN 10 and apply finance QoS. The practical result is identity-based segmentation: access follows who you are and the state of your device. A common misconception is that ISE stores AD credentials; it does not replicate user passwords. Instead, it queries AD or uses an intermediary for attribute checks. Example: a contractor account might be placed into a limited VLAN if not in the expected AD group. Troubleshooting AD integration commonly involves verifying LDAP connectivity, service account permissions, and correct group search bases. Takeaway: AD integration moves NAC from device-only policy to identity-aware enforcement, enabling more precise, least-privilege network access. Consider if your team has well-maintained AD groups to map directly into ISE policies before deployment.

keyIdea.title: Identity-driven policy
keyIdea.text: ISE uses AD group membership and attributes to apply dynamic policies such as VLAN assignment and access restrictions.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › ISE + Active Directory
How it works
ISE queries AD for user and group membership during authentication to evaluate policy. Decisions can then map users to VLANs, apply ACLs, or enforce remediation actions based on group attributes.
Policy example
If user is member of 'Finance_Group' and device is compliant, assign VLAN 10 and apply Finance QoS.
Troubleshoot tip
Verify LDAP bind credentials, search base, and that the ISE service account can read group membership. Check firewall rules for LDAP/S connections.
Concrete scenario
A contractor logs in; ISE checks AD and sees the account is not in an approved group, so it places the device in a restricted VLAN until manually approved or added to the correct group.
Key Takeaway

AD integration enables identity-aware access control, making NAC policies precise and operationally meaningful.

screens.title: Hands-on: Configure SW1 for 802.1X and MAB
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough ties configuration commands to observable outcomes so you can validate a working setup. Begin by enabling 'aaa new-model' and point dot1x authentication to a RADIUS server group for ISE. Define the RADIUS server with its IP and shared key, add it to a server-group, and enable 'dot1x system-auth-control' globally. On the interface, set 'authentication port-control auto' and choose host-mode depending on whether you expect multiple endpoints or voice/data split. Use 'authentication order dot1x mab' for laptop ports and 'authentication order mab dot1x' for legacy device ports. After configuration, verify connectivity by checking the switch for RADIUS server reachability and ISE logs for incoming requests. Test with a laptop supplicant and a printer using MAB to confirm both flows. A common diagnostic step is to check if UDP 1812 and 1813 traffic reaches the ISE IP; if not, check intermediate firewall rules and shared secret accuracy. Example verification commands include showing dot1x status, server-group reachability, and ISE authentication logs. Takeaway: configure one port first, validate both acceptance and rejection scenarios in ISE, and then expand systematically. What would you change first if the laptop never sends EAP messages?

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Lab: SW1
Starter CLI (SW1)
SW1>enable
SW1#configure terminal

! --- Global AAA and RADIUS Configuration ---
SW1(config)#aaa new-model
SW1(config)#aaa authentication dot1x default group ISE_RADIUS_GROUP
SW1(config)#aaa authorization network default group ISE_RADIUS_GROUP
SW1(config)#aaa accounting dot1x default start-stop group ISE_RADIUS_GROUP

SW1(config)#radius server ISE_SERVER
SW1(config-radius-server)#address ipv4 10.0.0.20 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
SW1(config-radius-server)#key CiscoISEKey!
SW1(config-radius-server)#exit

SW1(config)#aaa group server radius ISE_RADIUS_GROUP
SW1(config-sg-radius)#server name ISE_SERVER
SW1(config-sg-radius)#exit

SW1(config)#dot1x system-auth-control
After global config, apply per-interface commands for ports used by laptops and printers as in the template. Save configuration and monitor logs on ISE for incoming requests.
Validation checklist
  • Ping ISE from switch to confirm IP reachability.
  • Check UDP 1812/1813 access and shared secret consistency.
  • On ISE, watch incoming authentication attempts and their Accept/Reject outcome.
  • Test both EAP-based laptop and MAB printer flows to confirm correct VLAN assignment.
Key Takeaway

Deploy incrementally: one port, validate RADIUS and ISE logs, then scale configuration across the access layer.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: When deploying NAC, a few recurring issues cause the majority of failures. First, mismatched RADIUS shared secrets prevent the switch and ISE from decrypting or verifying messages; the symptom is that ISE reports malformed messages or the switch shows authentication server unreachable. Always verify the same secret on both sides. Second, network reachability and firewall rules frequently block UDP 1812 and 1813; if RADIUS packets cannot reach ISE, the authenticator will time out and keep the port unauthorized. Third, authentication order and host-mode settings on an interface can cause devices to be authenticated in the wrong method. For example, if MAB is attempted before 802.1X on a port intended for laptops, a laptop may be treated as a MAC device, losing user-based identity. Another common diagnostic error is assuming ISE stores passwords — it queries AD or LDAP for attributes and performs decision logic. Practical fixes include: test RADIUS with a simple UDP probe, enable verbose logging on the supplicant and switch, and use a single test port to iterate on configuration. Example troubleshooting sequence: verify switch-to-ISE ping, confirm shared secret, check ISE logs for Access-Request, and inspect supplicant logs for EAP messages. Takeaway: a methodical, layered check of connectivity, secrets, and interface settings will resolve most NAC deployment issues. Which of these checks will you run first in your environment?

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Troubleshooting
Top issues and diagnostics
Shared secret
Confirm identical keys on switch and ISE. Mismatch leads to rejects or malformed packets.
Network reachability
Verify UDP 1812/1813 reachability and firewall rules between switch and ISE.
Authentication order
Ensure dot1x vs mab order matches expected device types to avoid unintended fallbacks.
Suggested step sequence
  1. Ping ISE from the switch and verify UDP ports open.
  2. Check shared secret entries and re-enter if needed.
  3. Enable debug or verbose logs on supplicant and switch, then reproduce.
  4. Review ISE Auth logs for Access-Request and policy evaluation details.
Quick fixes
  • Re-enter RADIUS key and test immediately.
  • Temporarily allow UDP 1812/1813 for troubleshooting.
  • Use a test port and simple supplicant to isolate variables.
Key Takeaway

A layered diagnostic approach quickly exposes whether the fault is network, secret, or per-port misconfiguration.

NAC
Enforces policies on devices that attempt network connections so only authorized and compliant devices gain access.
802.1X
A port-based access control protocol that authenticates devices to a LAN or WLAN using EAP methods.
Supplicant
Client device requesting network access and running the 802.1X client software or supplicant.
Summary Takeaway

Keep these definitions handy as you configure devices and write policies; they form the vocabulary for NAC planning and troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Key Concepts
Authenticator
Switch or access point that controls the physical port and forwards EAP in RADIUS to ISE.
Policy Service Node
Runtime node in ISE that handles authentication and authorization requests from the network.
MAC Authentication Bypass
Fallback for non-802.1X devices that uses MAC address to authenticate against ISE; use sparingly.
One-line summary

Treat NAC as a combination of identity, posture, and access enforcement. Validate connectivity, secrets, and orders in a controlled lab before wide deployment.

fullNarratorScript:
Network Access Control is the practice of verifying and enforcing who and what can connect to your network. In modern enterprise environments, attackers can bypass perimeter controls by plugging into an access port or joining an open Wi-Fi. NAC adds a policy gate at every connection point so only authorized users and compliant devices can gain access. In this lesson you will see the 802.1X authentication model — supplicant, authenticator, and authentication server — and how Cisco Identity Services Engine centralizes policy decisions, posture checks, guest onboarding, and integration with Active Directory. You will also learn practical steps to configure a Cisco switch for 802.1X and MAC Authentication Bypass so legacy devices can still be controlled. We will highlight common mistakes such as wrong RADIUS secrets, blocked ports, or incorrect authentication order that can prevent devices from reaching the network. By the end of this chapter you will understand the components, the workflow, and a clear lab checklist to deploy basic NAC with ISE. Consider: which device types in your network must be treated as 802.1X-capable, and which will need MAB?

Over the next screens you will build a working mental model of Network Access Control and a practical checklist to configure it. First, you will learn to explain the purpose of NAC and why it is essential even in networks with strong perimeter controls. Then you will practice describing the 802.1X authentication actors — supplicant, authenticator, and authentication server — and how EAP messages travel through the network. You will also identify Cisco ISE core components and understand how they split responsibilities between policy administration, runtime decisions, and monitoring. Each objective is framed so you can both explain the concept and apply a basic configuration in a lab. For example, after studying the 802.1X objective you should be able to walk through a handshake and diagnose a failed port transition. Finally, these objectives prepare you to map business needs, like guest access and device onboarding, to ISE capabilities. Think about a device type in your network and how you would classify its access method under these objectives.

In this second objectives screen we focus on the operational and troubleshooting skills you will acquire. You will learn how ISE integrates with Active Directory to make policy decisions based on user group membership and how to design policies that combine identity and device posture. You will also practice configuring MAC Authentication Bypass so older devices can be authenticated by their MAC address, and you will understand the pros and cons of MAB compared to 802.1X. Finally, you will be equipped to troubleshoot common failures: incorrect RADIUS shared secrets, blocked firewall ports, and misordered authentication methods. Each objective here is framed for lab practice: configure the global AAA settings, add a RADIUS server and group, enable dot1x system-auth-control, and validate the authentication result. These skills let you both plan NAC deployments and debug them under pressure.

Network Access Control is a security approach that enforces policy each time a device or user attempts to connect to the network. At its core NAC asks two questions: who are you, and is your device compliant? If the answers meet policy, access is granted; if not, access is limited or denied. This prevents unmanaged or compromised devices from freely interacting with critical resources. For instance, if a laptop without updated antivirus plugs into an access switch, NAC can place it in a remediation VLAN until it meets compliance. A common misconception is treating NAC as only an identity check; in practice it combines identity, device posture, location, and time to make context-aware decisions. Another mistake is relying solely on perimeter controls — NAC enforces policy at the edge and reduces lateral movement during incidents. Example: a finance workstation should be placed in a VLAN with stricter access if it fails a posture check. Key takeaway: NAC is a gatekeeper at every access point that enforces who, what, and how devices connect. Consider which device groups in your network should be subject to the strictest NAC rules and why.

The 802.1X process is a handshake that gates a port until an authentication server trusts the device. First, the supplicant — the client device — initiates EAP messages when it detects a network connection. The authenticator, typically a switch or access point, intercepts those EAP frames and encapsulates them in RADIUS packets to forward to the authentication server. The server, often a RADIUS instance such as Cisco ISE, validates credentials and posture, then returns an Accept, Reject, or some attributes that the authenticator enforces. A key detail is port states: the authenticator keeps the port in an unauthorized state until it receives an Accept. A common example is a laptop that presents machine certificates via EAP-TLS; the server validates the certificate chain before accepting. Misconceptions often arise around who stores credentials — the RADIUS server holds or proxies identity stores, not the switch. Another pitfall is assuming EAP payloads transit unmodified; the authenticator encapsulates them in RADIUS so the server can perform policy mapping. Takeaway: understanding this three-party exchange helps you diagnose failures such as RADIUS rejects, timeouts, or ports stuck unauthorized. Try tracing a failed login: is the supplicant sending EAP, does the switch forward RADIUS, and what does the server log show?

Cisco Identity Services Engine is the centralized platform that makes policy decisions for network access. It separates concerns so each node type handles specific responsibilities. The Policy Administration Node, or PAN, is the management and configuration point where administrators author policies, define user and device profiles, and push configurations. The Policy Service Node — PSN — is the runtime engine that receives RADIUS requests from network devices, performs authentication and authorization, and returns decisions rapidly. For logging and reporting, the Monitoring and Troubleshooting Node, or MnT, collects logs and provides dashboards that help operators debug access issues and audit events. Optionally, Endpoint Protection Services handle additional endpoint security tasks. A common architecture is to place PANs centrally for management and deploy multiple PSNs near branch access points to reduce latency and improve redundancy. A misconception is to expect a single ISE node to handle both management and heavy runtime loads. In production, separating PAN from PSNs and MnT improves scalability and availability. Example: a PSN in a regional datacenter services hundreds of switches and forwards logs to the MnT. Takeaway: map policy administration, enforcement, and monitoring to distinct ISE roles for a scalable NAC deployment.

Configuring a Cisco switch for 802.1X and MAB begins with the global AAA and RADIUS server setup so the switch can reach ISE. You enable 'aaa new-model', point dot1x authentication to a RADIUS server group, and configure accounting if you need logs for sessions. Next, define the RADIUS server with its IP and shared key so the switch and ISE can communicate. Enabling 'dot1x system-auth-control' turns on 802.1X globally. For interface-specific behavior, set 'authentication port-control auto' to enable port-based control, choose 'authentication host-mode' appropriate to whether you expect phones and PCs on the same port, and set 'authentication order' to prefer dot1x or mab depending on the device mix. The 'mab' command enables MAC Authentication Bypass for legacy devices, and 'dot1x pae authenticator' sets the switch as the authenticator. A concrete example is setting 'authentication order dot1x mab' for a user laptop port, which tries 802.1X first and falls back to MAB if needed. A frequent mistake is mismatched RADIUS shared secrets or firewall rules blocking UDP 1812 and 1813. When you deploy, test with one port and watch ISE and switch logs for clear Accept or Reject messages. What command would you check first if the switch reports no response from the RADIUS server?

Deciding between 802.1X and MAC Authentication Bypass is about device capability and security needs. 802.1X provides strong, credential-based authentication using EAP methods and supports machine certificates and user credentials. It also allows posture assessment and clearer mapping to users and groups. MAB, by contrast, authenticates by MAC address and is intended for devices that cannot run an 802.1X supplicant, such as legacy printers or some IP phones. MAB is simpler but less secure because MAC addresses can be spoofed unless paired with additional checks in ISE. A sensible deployment pattern prioritizes 802.1X for managed endpoints and uses MAB only where necessary. Misconfiguration often comes from ordering authentication attempts incorrectly, which can lock out devices; for example, putting MAB first where you expect 802.1X devices may cause unintended MAB assignments. Example: use 'authentication order dot1x mab' on user laptop ports and 'authentication order mab dot1x' on printer ports. Takeaway: prefer 802.1X for security, reserve MAB for legacy devices, and explicitly document which ports use which order to prevent surprises during troubleshooting. Which device groups in your environment should be upgraded to 802.1X first?

Integrating Cisco ISE with Active Directory lets ISE query user and group attributes to make policy decisions. When ISE receives a RADIUS authentication request, it can perform an LDAP or AD lookup to determine group membership, user account status, and other attributes. This allows policies that say, for example, if a user is a member of 'Finance_Group' and the device posture is compliant, then assign VLAN 10 and apply finance QoS. The practical result is identity-based segmentation: access follows who you are and the state of your device. A common misconception is that ISE stores AD credentials; it does not replicate user passwords. Instead, it queries AD or uses an intermediary for attribute checks. Example: a contractor account might be placed into a limited VLAN if not in the expected AD group. Troubleshooting AD integration commonly involves verifying LDAP connectivity, service account permissions, and correct group search bases. Takeaway: AD integration moves NAC from device-only policy to identity-aware enforcement, enabling more precise, least-privilege network access. Consider if your team has well-maintained AD groups to map directly into ISE policies before deployment.
